title: One Wrong Signature and USCIS Keeps Your Money — The July 10 Rule Nobody Is Talking About
excerpt: A new USCIS regulation lets officers deny — not just reject — petitions with defective signatures, forfeiting filing fees with no chance to correct the error.
body:
A single missing wet-ink signature. That is all it will take for USCIS to deny your H-1B petition outright, pocket your filing fee, and send you back to the starting line.

On May 11, the agency published an interim final rule that codifies its authority to **deny** — not merely reject — immigration benefit requests that contain invalid signatures. The rule takes effect on July 10, 2026, and it applies to every petition filed on or after that date. For the roughly 344,000 people who filed H-1B petitions this year alone, most of them Indian nationals, the mechanics of this change matter more than the headlines suggest.

## Rejection versus denial — a $2,460 difference

Under existing practice, USCIS has two options when a filing arrives with a defective signature. Rejection means the package is returned unopened, the fee is refunded, and the applicant refiles. Inconvenient, but recoverable.

Denial is something else entirely. USCIS keeps the filing fee — currently $1,710 for the base I-129 petition, plus any applicable fraud prevention and ACWIA fees that can push the total past $2,460. The denial is recorded as a formal adjudication. The petitioner must file a brand-new petition, pay the full fee again, and start over. An appeal via Form I-290B costs an additional $800.

Until now, the regulations only addressed rejection for signature defects. The 2018 USCIS policy memo that authorised denials on signature grounds was guidance, not regulation. The new interim final rule turns that guidance into binding regulatory text with explicit fee-retention authority.

## What USCIS considers invalid

The rule does not change what counts as a valid signature — it changes the penalty for getting it wrong. Here is what the agency considers invalid:

- Copy-pasted or image-affixed signatures lifted from another document
- Typewritten names used as a substitute for a handwritten mark
- Stamped signatures, except in narrow enumerated circumstances
- Signatures by an unauthorised person, such as an attorney signing in place of the petitioner
- Signatures generated by software programs, including DocuSign and similar e-signature platforms

A scanned, faxed, or photocopied version of an originally signed document is acceptable — but only if the original bore a genuine wet-ink signature.

There is no cure provision. If USCIS accepts a petition, begins adjudicating it, and then discovers the signature is defective weeks or months later, it can deny the case without giving the petitioner a chance to correct the error. An officer may issue a Request for Evidence to confirm signatory authority, but not to invite submission of a corrected signature.

## The numbers behind the enforcement push

USCIS says it has seen a documented increase in invalid signatures in recent years, particularly signatures copied from other documents. Total denials on signature grounds rose from 300 in fiscal year 2021 to 2,953 in fiscal year 2025 — a nearly tenfold increase. The Administrative Appeals Office has adjudicated 758 appeals of copied-signature denials. The agency argues that because its intake procedures cannot catch many of these defects at the mailroom stage, officers sometimes reopen and readjudicate cases after significant work has already been performed.

The interim final rule went through without the standard notice-and-comment period. DHS is accepting public comments through July 10 — the same day the rule takes effect.

## What this means for Indian H-1B workers

Indians account for more than 70 per cent of all approved H-1B petitions. The practical exposure is enormous. Consider the typical chain: an employer files an I-129 petition for an H-1B worker, attaching a Labor Condition Application, supporting documentation, and multiple signature pages. The beneficiary signs in one place, the employer representative in another, the attorney in a third. A single defective signature anywhere in that stack — a DocuSign on the I-129, a typed name on the LCA — can trigger denial.

For workers already in the United States on H-1B status, the stakes are existential. A denied extension petition can leave someone out of status. A denied transfer petition can strand a worker between employers. A denied cap petition for FY2027, filed before the June 30 deadline, means the lottery slot is gone.

The rule also catches H-4 EAD applications, I-140 immigrant petitions, and adjustment-of-status filings. Every form filed with USCIS on or after July 10 is subject to the new enforcement framework.

## What to do before July 10

Immigration attorneys are advising clients to audit every signature workflow now. The checklist is short but unforgiving:

- Print every form, sign it by hand with a pen, then scan and submit
- Do not use DocuSign, Adobe Sign, or any e-signature platform for mailed or PDFi-filed petitions
- Confirm that employer representatives and attorneys are not signing on behalf of the petitioner unless specifically authorised
- For attorneys filing via USCIS's PDFi system, electronic signatures are not accepted — only a scanned wet-ink original
- Build signature verification into the filing process as a defined step before submission

The rule does not introduce a new standard. It introduces real consequences for an old one. The cost of ignoring it just became significantly harder to walk back.
